title: 170 Effects of corn silage supplementation while grazing Bermudagrass during late gestation with fall-calving cows
content:
Abstract
Forage management is one of the most important aspects to grazing operations. Through supplemental feeding, increasing nutrient availability and stocking rates have been known to increase productivity of cattle without increasing forage requirements. The objective of this study was to evaluate if supplemental feeding of corn silage impacted cow and calf performance during gestation while grazing Bermudagrass. Multiparous and primiparous Angus cross-bred fall-calving cows (n = 24; 547 ± 5.3 kg SEM; 5 ± 0.07 SEM BCS) averaging 146 ± 3 d of gestation at initiation of grazing were stratified by age (4.2 ± 0.5 yrs) and assigned to pasture (n = 3 cows/pasture). Treatment consisted of non-supplementation (NON) or supplementation (SUPP) fed daily at 1% of BW on DM basis (n = 4 pastures/treatment). Cows grazed from late May through mid-September (119 d). Body weight (BW), body condition score (BCS), hair score (HS), hair length (HL), ultrasound rump fat (RF), and serum cortisol measurements were taken at ~ middle of 2nd trimester, beginning of 3rd trimester, and approximately two weeks prior to parturition. Cows were weighed and BCS were taken at peak lactation. Calves were weighed at birth and used in weigh-suckle-weigh to estimate milk output. Forage accumulation (FA) and forage mass (FM) were estimated every 28 d using the paired-cage method. Cow-calf performance data was analyzed using PROC GLIMMIX in SAS 9.4 with pasture as experimental unit and cows within pastures as subsample. Forage mass and forage accumulation were analyzed using PROC GLIMMIX with pasture as experimental unit with repeated measures. Supplementation did not affect cow BW, BCS, HS, or HL during gestation (P > 0.13). During peak lactation, BCS (P > 0.35) and cow weights (P = 0.79) were not different. Calf birth weight was not affected by their dams being fed corn silage in late gestation (P = 0.91). Serum cortisol was affected by supplementation x cow age (P > 0.03) at the beginning of 3rd trimester. Non-supplemented young cows (primiparous) had greater serum cortisol levels than NON old (> 5 yrs) cows. Although visual BCS did not differ, cows that were SUPP measured a greater RF accumulation than NON cows through the end of the 2nd trimester (P = 0.06). Forage mass and forage accumulation did not differ (P > 0.78) based on supplementation method. Corn silage supplementation during late gestation, while cows graze growing Bermudagrass, had no physiological effects on cows or calves. Contrary to a previous year, supplementation had no effect on available forage.
